extraction.name: FLORES-101
extraction.description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and covering a variety of different topics and domains. These sentences have been translated into 101 languages by professional translators through a carefully controlled process. The resulting dataset enables better assessment of model quality on the long tail of low-resource languages, including the evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems, as all translations are multilingually aligned.
extraction.creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan
extraction.inLanguage: 101 languages including Afrikaans, Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Assamese, Asturian, Azerbaijani, Belarusian, Bengali, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Burmese, Catalan, Cebuano, Chinese (Simplified), Chinese (Traditional), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Filipino (Tagalog), Finnish, French, Fula, Galician, Ganda, Georgian, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hausa, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Igbo, Indonesian, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Javanese, Kabuverdianu, Kamba, Kannada, Kazakh, Khmer, Korean, Kyrgyz, Lao, Latvian, Lingala, Lithuanian, Luo, Luxembourgish, Macedonian, Malay, Malayalam, Maltese, Māori, Marathi, Mongolian, Nepali, Northern Sotho, Norwegian, Nyanja, Occitan, Oriya, Oromo, Pashto, Persian, Polish, Portuguese (Brazil), Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Shona, Sindhi, Slovak, Slovenian, Somali, Sorani Kurdish, Spanish (Latin America), Swahili, Swedish, Tajik, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Umbundu, Urdu, Uzbek, Vietnamese, Welsh, Wolof, Xhosa, Yoruba, Zulu
extraction.citeAs: Goyal, N., Gao, C., Chaudhary, V., Chen, P.-J., Wenzek, G., Ju, D., Krishnan, S., Ranzato, M., Guzmán, F., & Fan, A. (2021). The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The construction process consisted of three phases: (1) sourcing sentences to translate from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage), (2) designing and running pilot experiments to determine the translation process, and (3) launching the actual translation workflow for over 100 languages. Sentences were selected by randomly choosing an article from each source, then manually selecting 3-5 contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding very short or malformed sentences. The selection was balanced across beginning, middle, and end of articles. Translation was performed by professional Language Service Providers (LSPs) with a multi-step translation, automated quality check, and human evaluation process.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources: one third from Wikinews (international news articles), one third from Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children), and one third from WikiVoyage (travel guide articles).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Average of 26 days to translate 1 language, average of 35 days for re-translation, average of 61 days total for 1 language. Shortest turnaround was 31 days, longest was 89 days per language.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Several automatic checks were implemented: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether translation is a copy of the source sentence, (iii) checking whether translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, (v) checking whether translation is a copy from publicly available translation engines. A heuristic was used to detect copies from translation engines based on sentence-level spBLEU similarity (spBLEU > 50 against an engine's output, or difference > 20 between two engines). Translations with more than 10% violating sentences required re-translation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Sentences were translated by professional translators from selected Language Service Providers (LSPs). Translation workflow: sentences sent to translation LSP, then to different translators for editing, then automated quality control, then to evaluation LSP for human assessment. If the translation quality score was below 90%, translations were sent back for re-translation. The process could repeat for multiple rounds. Translation Quality Score is calculated per language on a 0-100 scale, determined based on identified errors (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register), each with severity (minor, major, critical).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Professional Language Service Providers (LSPs) - two translation LSPs and separate evaluation LSP
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation Quality Score was computed based on tallying error types and severities. Acceptable threshold set at 90%. About 50% of languages have fairly high quality (above 95%). The largest error category across all languages was mistranslation, including incorrect interpretation of source text, literal translations, and lack of disambiguation of ambiguous terms. Error categories with few errors included register, grammar, and punctuation. 45 languages required re-translation, with an average of 1 re-translation, up to 3 re-translations max.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each sentence translated by professional translators with editing, and quality-assured by independent LSP evaluators
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Sentence selection was performed by 10 different annotators in the lab, 6 male and 4 female, with different roles (researchers, scientists, engineers, program/project managers), originally coming from different regions: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America. Translators were professional translators from Language Service Providers.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SentencePiece (SPM) tokenizer with 256,000 tokens trained on monolingual data for spBLEU metric computation; sacrebleu; language identification tools; language models for fluency checking
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Dataset divided into three splits: dev (997 sentences from 281 articles), devtest (1012 sentences from 281 articles), and test (992 sentences from 280 articles). The dev and devtest are publicly downloadable, while the test set is available only via a publicly available evaluation server to guarantee equivalent assessment of models and reduce overfitting. Authors hope to continue expanding the number of languages covered and make the test set available to community efforts like WMT shared tasks.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages. The dataset enables evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems, supporting regionally-relevant language pairs like Spanish-Aymara and Vietnamese-Thai. The authors hope to foster progress in the machine translation community and beyond.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Source sentences are all from English Wikipedia, which may introduce translationese effects when translating from non-English languages. The authors conjecture these effects are marginal for low-resource language evaluation. Content is biased towards topics covered by Wikipedia (world travel, science, politics, crime). Sentence selectors came from specific regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, North America).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences are from English Wikipedia, which may produce translationese when evaluating non-English source translations. Language classification is complex and the chosen language family groupings are defined for analysis purposes only. Performance varies significantly by resource level and language family. Several languages were considered beyond the 101 but could not meet the 90% quality bar after rounds of re-translation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use case: Evaluation benchmark for machine translation (testing/evaluation), supporting many-to-many evaluation across 10,100 language pairs. Additional use cases: document-level translation, multimodal translation via images, sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation. The dev set is meant for hyper-parameter tuning, devtest for testing during development, and test (via evaluation server) for final assessment.
